fields.h1: Build a Speaker Application Form That Fills Your Agenda
fields.hero_description: Build a speaker application form that collects talk proposals and puts each one in front of the right reviewer.
fields.features_heading: What Reviewers Need From Every Proposal
fields.features_subheading: A speaker application form decides which talks reach the stage. This one also runs the review and the reply each speaker gets back.
fields.feature_1:
Questions that change with the format

Pick a workshop and the form asks for the seat limit and what attendees should bring. Pick a talk and it asks for the length, so nobody fills in a field that does not apply.
fields.feature_2:
Proposals sent to the right chair

Give each track an owner, and the app emails every proposal to the chair of the track it names. A proposal with no track goes to the program lead, so none sits unread.
fields.feature_3:
Scores with the speaker's name hidden

Reviewers read the title and abstract, score it on your scale, and add a note. Names stay hidden until every score is in, and the app averages them into one ranked list.
fields.feature_4:
Recording consent signed on the form

Ask speakers to agree that their session may be recorded and posted, and capture the signature with the proposal. The video crew finds consent in the same record as the talk.
fields.feature_5:
A proposal table with no response caps

Each proposal is saved as a row in a database you own, however many arrive before the deadline. Sort by track or average score, and mark each talk accepted or declined.
fields.feature_6:
The code, exported to your GitHub

On paid plans, export the full codebase of the form and its review screen to your GitHub repository. Run it beside your event site, or keep building on it for next year.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Events That Call for Speakers
fields.tab_content_1:
Solvig's Security talk goes straight to its chair

Pellmoor Dev Days gives every track its own chair. Its form asks for name, talk title, format, and track. Solvig Wetherell proposes Rotating CI secrets without downtime as a 30-minute talk in the Security track. The form then emails it to Ferdie Achterholt, the Security chair.
fields.tab_content_2:
Bao asks for March after all 3 slots are gone

The Wyndrift Data Meetup meets once a month and holds 3 lightning-talk slots of 5 minutes each. Speakers give their name, a talk title, and the month they want. Bao Lindqvar picks March after every March slot is taken. The form offers him the first April slot instead and holds his talk for that night.
fields.tab_content_3:
Matthis gets each travel request ahead of review

Matthis Brevitt runs the Corrowmere Freight Summit program on a fixed travel budget. Its form asks for name, company, home city, and whether travel needs covering. Any yes is flagged for Matthis before review. This week 4 speakers applied and 2 asked, Isobel Yarrick from Denver among them.
fields.tab_content_4:
With 3 blind scores in, a design talk makes the shortlist

Veska Lauwers chairs the program at the Fairmarsh UX Conference. Three reviewers score each proposal from 1 to 5 without seeing the speaker's name, and an average of 4 or higher makes the shortlist. Color contrast in charts scores 5, 4, and 4, an average of 4.3, and goes onto Veska's shortlist.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Speaker Application Form
fields.howto_description: Follow these 7 steps to build a speaker application form that brings in proposals and gets every one scored before the agenda is set.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 List the sessions your event runs
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Ask for what a reviewer scores
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Set the close date and slot count
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down the session types you accept, such as 30-minute talks and 90-minute workshops. Then name your tracks and give each one a chair, since every proposal will be routed by the track the speaker picks.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Collect the talk title, a short abstract, and the format. Cap the abstract at 250 words. Ask for a link to a past talk, and make it optional for anyone who has never spoken at an event.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Decide how many people score each proposal and on what scale, such as 3 reviewers scoring 1 to 5. Hide names until scoring ends. Then set the shortlist bar on that same scale, for example 4 or higher.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Choose the day the call for speakers closes and count the slots in each track or month. Decide what a proposal gets once its slot is full: a waitlist place or an offer of the next open date.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Put it all in one prompt
fields.howto_step_5_des: Describe the questions and the review rule in plain English. Emergent builds the speaker application form and the screen reviewers score on. Change a question later by asking.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Email each track chair when a proposal names their track, and send the program lead a weekly count. Every speaker gets a confirmation that says when decisions go out.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Submit one talk and one workshop from a spare email address. Check that each reaches the right chair, that the workshop asks for a seat limit, and that both rows appear in the table with no score yet.

faq_plan.q: What is a speaker application form?
faq_plan.a: A speaker application form is how an event collects proposals from people who want to give a talk. It asks who the speaker is, what the talk covers, and which format and track it fits. Organizers read and score the answers to decide who gets a place on the agenda.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a speaker application form?
faq_plan.a: Decide the formats you accept, the questions reviewers need answered, and how proposals get scored. Then describe all of it in one prompt to Emergent's AI form builder. It builds the form and the database behind it, and you change any question later by asking in plain English.

faq_plan.q: What questions should a speaker application form ask?
faq_plan.a: Start with the speaker's name and email, then a two-sentence bio. Then ask for the talk title, an abstract, the format, and the track. Add any access needs, such as captioning or step-free stage access. Leave headshots and slides until a talk is accepted.

faq_plan.q: Can one speaker application form take both talks and workshops?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Ask for the format first and branch from there, since a workshop needs answers a talk never does, such as room setup. Score the two formats in separate review rounds, and a talk never competes with a workshop for the same slot. If you also coach speakers one on one, screen those clients with a separate coaching application form.

faq_plan.q: How long should the abstract be on a speaker application form?
faq_plan.a: Cap it at 250 words. That leaves room for the problem, what the audience will learn, and one example, and keeps a stack of proposals readable in an evening. Put the limit beside the box, and ask for a one-line summary as well for the printed agenda.

faq_plan.q: How do I score speaker application forms without bias toward big names?
faq_plan.a: Hide each speaker's name and company in the first round, and judge only the title and abstract. Have at least 3 people score every proposal on the same five-point scale, then rank by the average. Emergent can build the review screen to keep names out of view until scoring closes.

faq_plan.q: Should a speaker application form ask about social media following?
faq_plan.a: Only if reach is part of how you choose speakers, and then say so on the form. If the program is about the talks, score the talk alone. When follower count is the main reason to invite someone, an influencer application form fits that job better.

faq_plan.q: When should a speaker application form close?
faq_plan.a: Count back from the day you plan to publish the agenda. Allow 2 weeks for scoring and 1 week for accepted speakers to confirm, and close the call before that. Print the close date on the form and in the confirmation email, and stop taking proposals on that date.

faq_plan.q: Should a speaker application form ask for a video of a past talk?
faq_plan.a: Ask for one, but keep it optional. A recording shows how someone holds a room, which an abstract cannot. Requiring it shuts out people who have never spoken. Offer them another route instead, such as a 2-minute phone video that walks through the talk.

faq_plan.q: How can a speaker application form encourage first-time speakers?
faq_plan.a: Add a checkbox for people who have never spoken at an event, and offer each one an experienced speaker to rehearse with. Run that pairing through a mentorship application form so mentors and new speakers match on topic. Emergent builds both from plain-English prompts, and the free tier covers building and publishing.

plan.angle: Pages for this term are template galleries whose speaker form stops at name, bio and a talk title. This page shows what an organizer does with each proposal once it arrives: a developer conference that emails each proposal to its track chair, a monthly meetup that offers the next month once 3 lightning slots fill, a freight summit that flags travel requests for the program lead, and a design conference where 3 reviewers score blind and an average of 4 makes the shortlist. The FAQ covers the definition, building one, which questions to ask, talks and workshops on one form, abstract length, blind review, audience size, close dates, past-talk videos and first-time speakers.
